title: {{NAME}} and the Herd That Played the Longest Game
moral: Play for the love of it, and you will find you are better than you ever knew.

pages.content:
The Mossfield, as the unicorns called it, had been used for their game since before any map had thought to name it. It was a valley between two slow hills, perfectly oval, perfectly green, and at its centre the grass was worn in a pattern that looked from above exactly like a football pitch, if football pitches had been invented by creatures made of light and speed.

{{NAME}} had followed a trail of silver hoofprints from the park behind his school. The hoofprints had begun appearing three days ago, faint and luminous, visible only from the corner of the eye. He had decided, this morning, to follow them properly.

The trail ended here. The Mossfield was empty except for a ball, sitting alone at the centre of the worn pitch, a perfectly ordinary football except for the fact that it glowed a very faint, pleased gold, as though quietly enjoying the morning sun.

pages.content:
They arrived from the trees on the western hill, first one, then three, then eleven, coming down the slope in a loose, unhurried herd that moved with the confident ease of creatures who owned this particular valley in the most complete possible way.

They were not like any unicorn {{NAME}} had imagined. They were large, larger than horses, their coats in every earth and sky colour, the leader a deep summer-storm grey with a horn of dark gold. They had the broad chests and powerful hindquarters of athletes, and they moved like a team that had been playing together for centuries.

The grey leader stopped in front of {{NAME}} and studied him with eyes the colour of amber resin. Then she nudged the glowing ball toward him with the flat of her nose.

"Oh," said {{NAME}}.

She waited.

"You need an even number," he said, working it out. "Eleven each side. You've got eleven. You need one more." He looked at the ball, then at her. "But I've only got one pair of boots."

Her ears swivelled forward. It appeared that one pair of boots was entirely sufficient.

pages.content:
The game was unlike anything {{NAME}} had played in his life, and he had played in a considerable number of games.

Unicorns, as it turned out, were extraordinary footballers. They could pass with the flat of their hoof with the precision of a billiard player. They read space intuitively. They communicated in a way that bypassed language entirely, some shared awareness of where everyone was at every moment, so that the game flowed like a single creature moving in complex patterns.

{{NAME}} was on the grey leader's team, which meant he had eleven very large, very capable teammates who nonetheless kept finding him in space with passes of extraordinary quality. He was, it quickly became clear, the designated finisher. And they trusted him to finish.

He didn't let them down. Two goals in the first half, both from passes so well-weighted that the finish was almost the easy part. He sprinted, slid, headed, and once, in a moment of pure impulse, bicycle-kicked a ball that was falling at exactly the wrong angle and connected with it so perfectly that the glowing gold of the ball briefly doubled.

The herd made a sound. Low, resonant, multi-layered. {{NAME}} decided it was the most extraordinary sound he had ever heard an audience make.

pages.content:
The score was even, three-three, with what the grey leader indicated with a slow turn of her head meant one more opportunity remaining. Not a minute. Not a set time. An opportunity. The game ran on its own logic.

The opposition's goalkeeper was a vast, white-coated unicorn whose horn blazed with a light that made it very difficult to judge where the goal actually ended. She was enormous and serene and appeared to have stopped twenty-seven shots without difficulty.

{{NAME}} received the ball in the final third. He had one shot. He understood this with the certainty of someone reading a chapter's last line.

He slowed. Breathed. Found the stillness inside the urgency.

The white goalkeeper had seen him do this twice before. Both times he had gone left. She shifted her weight left.

This time he went right, a check-and-drive so sudden and low that the ball skimmed the grass like a flat stone on water, curling at the last moment into the corner where the goal's light was weakest.

The grey lead unicorn reared. All eleven of her team reared with her, a wall of power and light and joy so large it blocked the sun for half a second.

It was, {{NAME}} thought, exactly enough.

pages.content:
Afterwards the herd grazed on the Mossfield, which was perhaps the most natural thing imaginable and also, in this context, the most companionable. {{NAME}} sat on the warm grass and watched them, the grey leader standing close, her large body warm and substantial beside him, both of them watching the afternoon settle into golden quiet.

She bent her head and pressed her dark gold horn very gently to the small silver horseshoe badge on his jersey. The badge glowed, just once, a soft warm pulse, and when the light faded it was fractionally more silver than before.

{{NAME}} touched it. Felt the warmth.

The hoofprint trail was still visible on the way home, but faint now, as though content rather than insistent. He followed them back through the park, through the long evening light.

He was in bed before the last of the gold had left the sky. The horseshoe badge was on his bedside table, still faintly warm against the wood.

He fell asleep with the low, resonant sound the herd had made still somewhere in his chest, like a kept promise.

In the morning, the hoofprints in the park were still there. A new trail. Heading somewhere he hadn't been yet.
